# TUI — Forms & Focus

### Rule 103 : Standardized form navigation

- `↑ / ↓` to navigate between a form's fields
- A visual indicator (`theme.IconCircleSmall`) must show the focused element
- `Enter` to validate action buttons only (see Rule 135)

### Rule 104 : Modal window structure

- Rounded border (NormalBorder) with color appropriate to the context
- Title at the top using `theme.TitleStyle`
- Message in the center
- Buttons at the bottom with consistent spacing
- Help instructions with `theme.HelpStyle` at the very bottom
- Safe choice by default (e.g. "No" for delete confirmations)

### Rule 113 : Form field spacing

| Layout | Separator after the field |
|--------|--------------------------|
| **Multi-line**: label ↵ content | `\n\n` (blank line) |
| **Single-line**: label + content on the same line | `\n` |
| **Checkboxes** | `\n` between them, `\n\n` after the group |

`renderField()` functions must **NOT** include the trailing separator.

### Rule 114 : Built-in help system (`?`)

**Every view implements `help.Provider` via `GetHelpContent()`, always in English.**

Obligations:
- Mandatory update in the same commit whenever a feature / keybinding changes
- Every new view must implement `help.Provider` with complete content

Expected content: `Title`, `Description`, `KeyBindings`, `Sections`

Files:
- `internal/ui/help/help.go` — component and `Provider` interface
- `internal/ui/*/view.go` or `model.go` — per-view implementation

### Rule 120 : Focus indicator and form field rendering

**Indentation: 2 characters.** When focused, `theme.IconCircleSmall` sits at column 0.

| State | Prefix |
|------|---------|
| Focused | `IconCircleSmall + " "` → `● Label` |
| Not focused | `"  "` (2 spaces) → `  Label` |

`theme.IconCircleSmall` (`\ueb8a`) does NOT contain a space — always add `" "` after it.

**Label/value separator**: `theme.IconChevronRight` (`\uf054`) + `" "`. **No `:`**.

**A space before the chevron is mandatory**: there must always be a space between the label text and `IconChevronRight`.

```go
// ✅ Single-line, focused
theme.KeyStyle.Render(theme.IconCircleSmall + " Server " + theme.IconChevronRight + " ") + input.View()

// ✅ Multi-ligne
theme.KeyStyle.Render(theme.IconCircleSmall + " Name " + theme.IconChevronRight) + "\n"
theme.Bg("  ") + input.View()

// ❌ WRONG — no space before the chevron
theme.KeyStyle.Render(theme.IconCircleSmall + " Name" + theme.IconChevronRight) + "\n"
theme.KeyStyle.Render("▸ Server: ") + input.View()
```

**Selection lists**: `IconCircleSmall` for the selected item, `"  "` for the others.

**Focus color**: `theme.ColorHighlight` for all field types.

**TextInput cursor**: configure via `theme.StyleTextInput(&myInput)` (sets `Prompt = ""`).

**Checkboxes**: via `theme.RenderCheckbox()`.

**There are no radio buttons.** For a closed set of values, the control is
the `←→` cycle field (Rule 132) — regardless of how many values there are,
even two. `theme.RenderRadioButton()` was removed along with its last two
callers (§3.9 of the backlog); recreating it locally is forbidden.

Forbidden:
- ❌ `▸` as a focus indicator (use `theme.IconCircleSmall`)
- ❌ `:` as the label/value separator (use `theme.IconChevronRight`)
- ❌ `ColorPrimary` for focused elements (use `ColorHighlight`)
- ❌ Recreating `RenderCheckbox` locally
- ❌ Reintroducing radio buttons, in any form

### Rule 131 : Top padding for forms in the viewport

**Every form displayed in the main viewport must begin with exactly one blank line (1-line top padding).**

```go
// ✅ CORRECT — a single blank line
func (f *Form) View() string {
    return theme.EmptyLineBg(f.width) + "\n" +
        f.renderFields()
}

// ❌ WRONG — two blank lines (EmptyLineBg + "\n\n")
func (f *Form) View() string {
    return theme.EmptyLineBg(f.width) + "\n\n" + f.renderFields()
}

// ❌ WRONG — form stuck to the viewport's top edge
func (f *Form) View() string {
    return f.renderFields()
}
```

Does not apply to modals (positioned via `lipgloss.Place`).

### Rule 132 : Closed-list fields (value cycling)

**Any field whose value belongs to a finite set must use the ←→ cycle pattern.**

It is the **only** control allowed for a closed set. Radio buttons are not
an alternative for two or three values: they no longer exist in the
application (Rule 120). Checkboxes remain for independent booleans, which is
a different thing from an exclusive choice.

#### Visual

```
  Visibility  󰅂 private        ← not focused
● Visibility  󰅂 internal       ← focused (KeyStyle)
```

Line structure:

| Part | Value |
|--------|--------|
| Focus indicator | `theme.IconCircleSmall + " "` (focused) or `"  "` (not focused) |
| Label | field text, e.g. `"Visibility"` |
| Selection icon | `" " + theme.IconSelect + " "` |
| Separator | `theme.IconChevronRight + " "` |
| Current value | plain text with `ColorText` |

#### Navigation

- `←` / `→`: move to the previous / next value (cycling)
- `Tab` / `Shift+Tab`: navigate to the previous / next field

Do not use `Enter` to cycle — `Enter` confirms the form or advances to the next field.

#### Reference implementation

```go
// Rendu
func (f *Form) renderCycleField(label string, options []string, idx int, fieldIdx int) string {
    selectLabel := label + " " + theme.IconSelect + " "
    value := lipgloss.NewStyle().Background(theme.ColorBackground).Foreground(theme.ColorText).Render(options[idx])
    if f.focusedField == fieldIdx {
        return theme.KeyStyle.Render(theme.IconCircleSmall+" "+selectLabel+theme.IconChevronRight+" ") + value
    }
    return theme.Bg("  "+selectLabel+theme.IconChevronRight+" ") + value
}

// Key handling
case "left":
    if f.focusedField == fieldIdx {
        f.idx = (f.idx - 1 + len(f.options)) % len(f.options)
    }
case "right":
    if f.focusedField == fieldIdx {
        f.idx = (f.idx + 1) % len(f.options)
    }
```

Forbidden:
- ❌ Using `Enter` to cycle values
- ❌ Opening a dropdown list for 2–4 values (reserve that for long lists, cf. `renderTemplateList`)
- ❌ Hardcoding the value's color (use `ColorText`)
- ❌ Using radio buttons for a closed set (Rule 120)

### Rule 121 : Circular iconography for statuses

Status indicators in tables and lists must use circular icons:

| State | Icon |
|------|-------|
| Success / OK | `theme.IconOK` (`\uf058`) |
| Error / Failure | `theme.IconError` (`\uf057`) |
| Warning | `theme.IconWarning` (`\uf071`) |

Applies to: scan results, pipeline statuses, UP/DOWN indicators.
Does not apply to: object-type icons (folders, files, GitLab logo).

### Rule 133 : Multi-line text fields — `WrappedInput` mandatory

**`bubbles/textarea` is forbidden.** Its internal background is not controllable by lipgloss and produces visual artifacts (a `┃` gutter, terminal background between lines).

Use **`components.WrappedInput`** (`internal/ui/components/wrapped_input.go`) for any text field that must display across multiple lines.

#### API

```go
// Creation
field := components.NewWrappedInput(wrapWidth, charLimit, "placeholder text")

// Resizing — call inside the tea.WindowSizeMsg handler
field.SetDisplayWidth(terminalWidth)

// Focus / Blur
field.Focus()   // called from updateFocus()
field.Blur()    // called from updateFocus()

// Dans Update() — passer les messages clavier quand le champ a le focus
field, cmd = field.Update(msg)

// In View() — returns the multi-line content block, ready to concatenate
return labelStr + "\n" + field.View()

// Retrieving the value on submit
value := field.Value()
```

#### `wrapWidth` parameter

`wrapWidth` is the number of **runes** per visual line before wrapping (word-wrap at the last space, hard-break if there is no space).

| Context | Recommended value |
|----------|--------------------|
| GitLab description (group/project) | `80` |
| Short notes field | `60` |
| Long text field | `100` |

```go
// ✅ CORRECT
const descWrapWidth = 80
descInput := components.NewWrappedInput(descWrapWidth, 250, "description (optional)")

// ❌ WRONG
descInput := textarea.New()
```

#### Behavior

- Empty field + focused → only the block cursor is shown
- Empty field + not focused → placeholder in `ColorDim`
- Filled field → word-wrapped text, each line padded with `theme.PadWithBg` up to `displayWidth`
- Inverted block cursor (`ColorText` bg / `ColorBackground` fg) at the exact caret position

Forbidden:
- ❌ `bubbles/textarea` in any view
- ❌ Recreating the word-wrap or cursor logic locally
- ❌ Forgetting to call `SetDisplayWidth` in the `tea.WindowSizeMsg` handler

### Rule 135 : Strict keybinding assignment in forms ⚠️

**Every key has a single, unambiguous role.** These rules apply to every form in the application without exception.

| Key | Exclusive role |
|--------|---------------|
| `↑ / ↓` | Navigate between a form's fields |
| `Tab / Shift+Tab` | Switch between tabs **only** — never for navigation between fields |
| `Space` | Toggle a checkbox — the **only** key allowed for this role |
| `Enter` | Validate an action button or trigger a specific action — **never** to toggle a checkbox |
| `← / →` | Change level in a table (drill-down/up) **and** cycle the values of a closed-list field |
| `Esc` | Cancel / close / return to the parent level |

#### Detailed rules

**`Tab / Shift+Tab` — tabs only**
- Reserved for switching between tabs (`bubbles/table` breadcrumb, result tabs, etc.)
- Must **never** be used to move forward/backward between form fields
- If a view has no tabs, `Tab` must do nothing (or be ignored)

**`↑ / ↓` — navigation between fields**
- The only keys to move focus from one field to another in a form
- In a list/table outside a form: row-by-row movement (Rule 111)

**`Space` — toggle checkbox**
- The only valid key to check/uncheck a checkbox
- `Enter` on a checkbox must be ignored or advance to the next field, never toggle it

**`Enter` — validation / action**
- Validates the currently focused button
- Triggers a contextual action (e.g. launch a scan, open a detail view)
- Must **not** toggle a checkbox

**`← / →` — table navigation and value cycling**
- In a table: `←` moves up a level (drill up), `→` moves down a level (drill down)
- On a closed-list field (cycle field): `←` previous value, `→` next value (Rule 132)
- Must **not** move focus between form fields

#### Common violations to avoid

```go
// ❌ WRONG — Tab to navigate between fields
case "tab":
    m.focusedField = (m.focusedField + 1) % fieldCount

// ❌ WRONG — Enter to toggle a checkbox
case "enter":
    if m.focusedField == fieldMyCheckbox {
        m.myCheckbox = !m.myCheckbox
    }

// ✅ CORRECT — Space to toggle
case " ":
    if m.focusedField == fieldMyCheckbox {
        m.myCheckbox = !m.myCheckbox
    }

// ✅ CORRECT — ↑/↓ to navigate between fields
case "up":
    m.focusedField = max(m.focusedField-1, 0)
case "down":
    m.focusedField = min(m.focusedField+1, fieldCount-1)
```

176	## The socket table — `internal/ports`
177	
178	The machine's TCP and UDP sockets, and the process holding each, read **in this
179	process**. `List(ctx, resolve)` and `Kill(pid)` are the whole interface.
180	
181	**It exists because the old one answered for the wrong machine** (D55). The
182	Ports tab ran `ss -tupan` inside
183	`docker run --rm --net=host --pid=host --privileged`, and on Docker Desktop
184	`--net=host` is the namespace of the Linux VM: the tab listed the VM's NFS
185	daemons with two-digit PIDs while not one of the host's 38 listening sockets
186	appeared, and `K` sent SIGKILL to a process of the VM under the impression it was
187	freeing a port on the machine. The sentence explaining this has sat at the top of
188	`docker.runDiagHost` since §3.33 rapatriated DNS, ICMP, TCP, TLS and HTTP for
189	exactly the same reason; `RunSS` and `KillProcess` were the two nobody pulled it
190	for. **Under Linux the defect did not exist**, which is why it went unnoticed:
191	the tab was right on the platform it was written on.
192	
193	No new dependency: `gopsutil/v4/net` was already imported by
194	`internal/metrics/host.go`. Windows reads iphlpapi, Linux `/proc`, macOS and the
195	BSDs `lsof` — the last is a subprocess, but one the system supplies, and it
196	replaces a privileged container.
197	
198	Four decisions, each with a test:
199	
200	- **The process names come from one enumeration, not one call per socket.** The
201	  obvious `process.NewProcess(pid).Name()` goes through `OpenProcess` on
202	  Windows and needs rights over the target: measured here, **98 of 189** sockets
203	  came back *Access denied*, so the Process column would have been empty for

## The socket table — `internal/ports`

The machine's TCP and UDP sockets, and the process holding each, read **in this
process**. `List(ctx, resolve)` and `Kill(pid)` are the whole interface.

**It exists because the old one answered for the wrong machine** (D55). The
Ports tab ran `ss -tupan` inside
`docker run --rm --net=host --pid=host --privileged`, and on Docker Desktop
`--net=host` is the namespace of the Linux VM: the tab listed the VM's NFS
daemons with two-digit PIDs while not one of the host's 38 listening sockets
appeared, and `K` sent SIGKILL to a process of the VM under the impression it was
freeing a port on the machine. The sentence explaining this has sat at the top of
`docker.runDiagHost` since §3.33 rapatriated DNS, ICMP, TCP, TLS and HTTP for
exactly the same reason; `RunSS` and `KillProcess` were the two nobody pulled it
for. **Under Linux the defect did not exist**, which is why it went unnoticed:
the tab was right on the platform it was written on.

No new dependency: `gopsutil/v4/net` was already imported by
`internal/metrics/host.go`. Windows reads iphlpapi, Linux `/proc`, macOS and the
BSDs `lsof` — the last is a subprocess, but one the system supplies, and it
replaces a privileged container.

Four decisions, each with a test:

- **The process names come from one enumeration, not one call per socket.** The
  obvious `process.NewProcess(pid).Name()` goes through `OpenProcess` on
  Windows and needs rights over the target: measured here, **98 of 189** sockets
  came back *Access denied*, so the Process column would have been empty for
  every service on the box. `Processes()` reads a Toolhelp32 snapshot instead
  and named **294 of 294** in 11 ms, elevated or not. The bulk call is not an
  optimisation over the per-PID one — it is the difference between a column that
  is filled in and one that is not.
- **A PID of zero carries no PID.** It is the system declining to attribute the
  socket, and `K` keys on that field: left as `"0"` the row would look killable,
  and process 0 is a whole process group on Unix. `Kill` refuses it a second
  time, on the model of §3.23's double guard. The name is a *separate* question:
  a row may know which process holds the socket and not what it is called, and
  it must stay killable — that is the row the user is acting on.

  datagram socket is `NONE` on Linux and nothing at all on Windows, so the same
  socket read differently depending on where DevDesk ran — and the `l`/`e`
  filters with it. `ESTABLISHED` is shortened to `ESTAB` because the State
  column is ten cells wide, so the long spelling renders as `ESTABLISHE`.

  that would mean shipping a copy of `/etc/services` and calling the result the

1	package app
2	
3	import (
4		"errors"
5		"log"
6		"net"
7		"net/http"
8	
9		tea "github.com/charmbracelet/bubbletea"
10	
11		"github.com/anthnel/devdesk/internal/command"
12		"github.com/anthnel/devdesk/internal/config"
13		mcpserver "github.com/anthnel/devdesk/internal/mcp"
14		"github.com/anthnel/devdesk/internal/ui/components"
15		"github.com/anthnel/devdesk/internal/ui/configuration"
16	)
17	
18	// MCPServerStartedMsg reports what became of the attempt to serve MCP.
19	//
20	// It is a message and not a return value because opening a listener is I/O, and
21	// I/O belongs in a Cmd (Rule 110). Addr is what the listener actually bound —
22	// not what the setting asked for — so a port chosen by the OS would be reported
23	// truthfully; Err is why there is nothing listening.
24	type MCPServerStartedMsg struct {
25		// Epoch is which start this reports. A switch made while an earlier start
26		// is still in flight — ResolveToken can block on a locked keyring, or on a
27		// two-second `git config` read — would otherwise have the old start's
28		// message land afterwards and store its server, leaving a listener still
29		// answering for the context nobody is in while the new one fails to bind.
30		// That is exactly the guarantee the restart exists to give.
31		Epoch  uint64
32		Addr   string
33		Server *http.Server
34		Err    error
35		// Token is the bearer an agent has to present. It is carried here so the
36		// configuration view can show it — the one screen where somebody goes
37		// looking for it — and it lives in the secret store, never in a file
38		// DevDesk writes (§3.9).
39		Token string
40	}
41	
42	// startMCPCmd is a method so it reads the router's config, context and secret
43	// store; those three are copied into the closure rather than read from the
44	// receiver inside it, because a Cmd runs on its own goroutine and the receiver
45	// is the model (Rule 110).
46	
47	// startMCPCmd serves this context over MCP, or explains why it does not.
48	//
49	// Nothing is attempted when the context has not enabled it: the refusal is
50	// carried on the message rather than logged and dropped, because "off" and
51	// "could not bind" look identical from the outside and only one of them is a
52	// problem.
53	//
54	// The listener is opened here, inside the Cmd, and handed back on the message.
55	// That is the same shape as a scan's context.CancelFunc travelling on its
56	// starting message: the thing is created where the I/O happens and stored by
57	// the one place allowed to store it.
58	func (a *App) startMCPCmd() tea.Cmd {
59		a.mcpEpoch++
60		epoch := a.mcpEpoch
61	
62		cfg := a.config
63		contextName := a.currentContext
64		secrets := a.sharedState.Secrets
65		dispatch := a.mcpDispatch
66	
67		return func() tea.Msg {
68			if !cfg.MCP.Enabled {
69				return MCPServerStartedMsg{Epoch: epoch, Err: mcpserver.Refused(contextName)}
70			}
71	
72			addr := cfg.MCP.Listen
73			if addr == "" {
74				addr = config.DefaultMCPListen
75			}
76	
77			// Before the listener, not after: a port that answers without a token
78			// is what this whole step exists to prevent, and binding first would
79			// open one for the width of the failure path.
80			token, err := mcpserver.ResolveToken(secrets)
81			if err != nil {
82				return MCPServerStartedMsg{Epoch: epoch, Err: err}
83			}
84	
85			handler, err := mcpserver.Handler(&mcpserver.Env{
86				Config:   cfg,
87				Context:  contextName,
88				Dispatch: dispatch,
89			})
90			if err != nil {
91				return MCPServerStartedMsg{Epoch: epoch, Err: err}
92			}
93			handler = mcpserver.Authorize(handler, token)
94	
95			ln, err := net.Listen("tcp", addr)
96			if err != nil {
97				return MCPServerStartedMsg{Epoch: epoch, Err: err}
98			}
99	
100			srv := &http.Server{Handler: handler}
101			go func() {
102				// ErrServerClosed is what Shutdown produces, so it is the ordinary
103				// end of a session and not a failure. Anything else happened to a
104				// server the user believed was up, and the log is the only place
105				// left to say so — the footer's message is three seconds long and
106				// this can arrive an hour in.
107				if err := srv.Serve(ln); err != nil && !errors.Is(err, http.ErrServerClosed) {
108					log.Printf("ERROR [app/mcp] serve: %v", err)
109				}
110			}()
111	
112			return MCPServerStartedMsg{Epoch: epoch, Addr: ln.Addr().String(), Server: srv, Token: token}
113		}
114	}
115	
116	// restartMCPCmd serves the context now on screen, and stops serving the one that
117	// was (§3.61).
118	//
119	// The server is built around one Env — a config and a context name captured
120	// when it starts — so a switch that left it running would keep answering for
121	// the context nobody is in any more. Rebuilding is not a nicety here; not doing
122	// it is the bug.
123	//
124	// **The restart drops the open MCP sessions, and that is the guarantee, not a
125	// side effect.** §3.38 fixed the context at process start precisely so it could
126	// not change underneath an agent mid-conversation; §3.61 gives that up, and
127	// what replaces it is this — a client does not silently start reading another
128	// context, it loses its session and re-initialises. The alternative on offer
129	// was a notification, and the SDK only delivers one if the client has set a log
130	// level, which is a guarantee that holds when it feels like it.
131	//
132	// Switching to a context with `mcp.enabled: false` therefore stops the server:
133	// the setting is per context, and a server outliving the context that allowed
134	// it would be the one way to serve a context that said no.
135	func (a *App) restartMCPCmd() tea.Cmd {
136		srv := a.mcpServer
137		a.mcpServer = nil
138		a.mcpAddr = ""
139		a.mcpErr = nil
140		a.mcpToken = ""
141	
142		start := a.startMCPCmd()
143		if srv == nil {
144			return start
145		}
146		return tea.Sequence(
147			func() tea.Msg {
148				// Close rather than Shutdown: an agent's request in flight belongs
149				// to the context being left, and letting it finish would answer for
150				// that context after the user has moved on — which is the thing
151				// this restart exists to prevent.
152				_ = srv.Close()
153				return nil
154			},
155			start,
156		)
157	}
158	
159	// handleMCPServerStarted stores the running server, or records why there is
160	// none.
161	//
162	// Both outcomes are kept. A view that wants to tell the user where to point an
163	// agent needs the address; one that wants to say why nothing is listening needs
164	// the error, and "the setting is off" is one of the answers rather than the
165	// absence of one.
166	func (a *App) handleMCPServerStarted(msg MCPServerStartedMsg) (tea.Model, tea.Cmd) {
167		// A report from a start the session has moved past. Its listener, if it got
168		// one, is closed here rather than stored: storing it would leave a server
169		// answering for a context nobody is in, and dropping it silently would leak
170		// the port the current context is trying to bind.
171		if msg.Epoch != a.mcpEpoch {
172			if msg.Server != nil {
173				log.Printf("MCP server for a superseded context closed on arrival (epoch %d, now %d)", msg.Epoch, a.mcpEpoch)
174				_ = msg.Server.Close()
175			}
176			return a, nil
177		}
178	
179		a.mcpServer = msg.Server
180		a.mcpAddr = msg.Addr
181		a.mcpErr = msg.Err
182		a.mcpToken = msg.Token
183	
184		// The configuration view shows all three, and it is built lazily — so drop
185		// the cached one and let it be rebuilt with what is now true. The precedent
186		// is useSecrets rebuilding the auth view when the store is resolved.
187		//
188		// Rebuilt at once when it is the screen the user is on, and not merely
189		// dropped: renderBody falls back to "View not found: configuration" for a
190		// currentView with no entry, and keys.go routes nothing to it — the user
191		// would sit on a dead screen until they retyped `:config`. Reachable two
192		// ways: `app.default_view: configuration` plus the startup report, which
193		// fires even when the server is off, and a context switch made while
194		// sitting in that view.
195		if _, cached := a.views[command.ViewConfiguration]; cached {
196			delete(a.views, command.ViewConfiguration)
197			if a.currentView == command.ViewConfiguration {
198				a.createView(command.ViewConfiguration)
199				a.resize(a.width, a.height)
200			}
201		}
202	
203		if msg.Err != nil {
204			log.Printf("MCP server not serving context %q: %v", a.currentContext, msg.Err)
205			// Only when the context asked for a server. Nothing was attempted
206			// otherwise, so there is nothing to report, and a message announcing
207			// the failure of a server nobody asked for reads as a fault (§3.61).
208			//
209			// Rule 128 calls this an Error and not a Warn: the bind was refused,
210			// which is the system saying no, not an action that cannot be honoured
211			// as asked. The commonest cause is a second `dk` already holding the
212			// port — the TUI keeps running without a server, because losing the
213			// application over a taken port would be out of all proportion.
214			if !a.config.MCP.Enabled {
215				return a, nil
216			}
217			return a, components.PostFooter(components.LevelError, "MCP server not started — "+msg.Err.Error())
218		}
219		log.Printf("MCP server for context %q listening on %s", a.currentContext, msg.Addr)
220		return a, nil
221	}
222	
223	// mcpFacts is what the configuration view shows about the server: where it
224	// listens, the bearer an agent needs, or why there is nothing.
225	//
226	// The refusal is rendered rather than the error value, because "the setting is
227	// off" is one of the answers and reads as a state, not a fault.
228	func (a *App) mcpFacts() configuration.MCPFacts {
229		facts := configuration.MCPFacts{Addr: a.mcpAddr, Token: a.mcpToken}
230		if a.mcpErr != nil && a.config.MCP.Enabled {
231			facts.Reason = a.mcpErr.Error()
232		}
233		return facts
234	}

|---|---|

| `viewNames` map — canonical name **and** every alias | `parser.go:85-118` |
| `routerViews` — only if the view is router-opened and *not* typeable (like `ViewViewer`) | `parser.go:59` |

Key rule, `parser.go:79-84`: `viewNames` is **the single source for both parsing and completion**. The map key equal to the `ViewType` string *is* the full name; every other key is an alias. So `:net`/`netdiag` → `ViewNetdiag` is just two entries:
```go

"net":           ViewNetdiag,
```

Nothing else is needed for completion — `CompletionEngine.buildCommands()` (`internal/command/completion.go:29-57`) derives suggestions from `FullNames()` + `GetAliases()`, which both read `viewNames`.

The three derived lists and who consumes them:

- `ViewNames()` — `parser.go:205-214`: canonical typeable names. Feeds `app.default_view` (`internal/app/app.go:236-245` → `command.Parse`) and the configuration view's `default_view` cycle field (`internal/ui/configuration/model.go:137`, `internal/ui/configuration/forge.go:50`).
- `AllViewNames()` — `parser.go:224-231`: `ViewNames()` + `routerViews`. **This is what the router's contract tests iterate.**

## 2. `internal/app/` — the router

### The interfaces a view must satisfy (verbatim)

**Mandatory** — `internal/app/app_header.go:12-18`:
```go
// HeaderView is the interface each view must implement to provide the header data
type HeaderView interface {
	GetShortcuts() shortcut.Shortcuts
	GetTitle() string
	GetIcon() string
	GetHeaderInfo(context string) []shortcut.HeaderInfo
}
```

**Mandatory in practice (Rule 124)** — `internal/app/app_header.go:20-25`:
```go
// FooterView is implemented by views that have footer content rendered below the viewport border (Rule 124).
// The footer can contain a tab bar (1 line) and optionally an empty line + info line (2 lines).
type FooterView interface {
	GetFooterHeight() int          // current footer height in lines (0 if no footer)
	RenderFooter(width int) string // rendered footer content
}
```

**Mandatory (Rule 114)** — `internal/ui/help/help.go:31-34`:
```go
// Provider is the interface views must implement to provide help

	GetHelpContent() Content
}
```

**Optional, probed silently** — `internal/app/app_header.go:27-36`:
```go

	Frameless() bool
}
```
`internal/app/app.go:31-35`:
```go
// FormView interface for views that can have active forms
// Views implementing this interface can prevent command mode activation
type FormView interface {
	InEditMode() bool
}
```
`internal/app/app.go:37-51`:
```go
type LeavingView interface {
	Leave() (tea.Model, tea.Cmd, bool)
}
```
`internal/app/app.go:53-58`:
```go
// FilterBarView is implemented by views that have a visible filter bar.
// When the filter bar is visible, the viewport bottom border corners are
// replaced with T-junction chars (├/┤) to form a closed rectangle.
type FilterBarView interface {
	FilterBarVisible() bool
}
```

Plus the base `tea.Model` (`Init/Update/View`) — `views` is `map[command.ViewType]tea.Model` (`app.go:68`).

### Construction and caching

- **`createView`** — `internal/app/command_line.go:162-201`. One `case` per `ViewType` in a switch. **A missing case builds nothing and the contract test fails with "the switch has no case for it".** Note the guard at `:164`: already-built views are skipped *except* `ViewGitAuth`, which is always rebuilt.
- **Lazy loading**: `switchView` (`command_line.go:111-137`) calls `createView` only if absent, then `tea.Batch(newView.Init(), a.requestResize(), a.sendJobsTo(view))`.
- **Eagerly built at startup**: dashboard, status, and the landing view — `app.go:224-226`.
- **Settling before leaving**: `switchView:114-117` calls `settleCurrentView()` (`command_line.go:148-160`), which probes `LeavingView`; a `false` cancels the switch.
- **Selection-mode reset**: `resetSelectionModeFor` (`command_line.go:98-109`) drops the workspaces view before switching to it.

- **`layoutOnce`** — `app.go:298-327`, the exact budget:

  ```go
  footerHeight := a.getFooterHeight()
  a.lastFooterHeight = footerHeight
  headerHeight := lipgloss.Height(a.renderHeader())
  ```

**`/c/.../internal/ui/keymap/keymap.go`**

```go
// free lists the uppercase letters no action occupies. They are declared
// rather than left to be inferred: the next addition must know where to
// pick from without redoing the survey, and an action that settles
// somewhere other than here is a duplicate that goes unnoticed.
// H came back here with §3.47 (it used to trace the route, removed because
// it answered for the Docker VM rather than for the machine, D57) and left
// again with Diagnose (§3.66): a good semantic fit for "look closer at this
// target's network path." A letter an action has just freed up is
// re-declared free, otherwise it stays reserved for a use that no longer

var free = []string{"J", "Q", "Z"}
```

**The free letters are `J`, `Q`, `Z` — three of them.** The 23 declared actions are at `keymap.go:56-83` (`N E D M S A F C T O W L V K P B G U X R I H Y`). The invariant `len(actions) + len(free) == 26` is enforced by `TestFreeLettersAreActuallyFree` (`keymap_test.go:79-89`) — so **you cannot add a new action without removing a letter from `free`, and vice versa.**

### `localToggles` — `keymap.go:198-222`

```go
var localToggles = []Surface{
	{"containers", "ui/containers/", []string{"r", "p", "s", "t", "z"}},
	{"viewer", "ui/viewer/", []string{"f", "c", "w", "v", "t", "n", "g", "s"}},
	{"netdiag/ports", "ui/netdiag/ports_model.go", []string{"t", "u", "l", "e", "n", "z"}},
	{"netdiag/checks", "ui/netdiag/", []string{"p"}},
	{"oci/browser", "ui/oci_resources/browser_", []string{"r"}},
	{"security/findings", "ui/security/", []string{"c", "h", "m", "l"}},
```

`Surface` is `{Name, Path, Keys}` (`keymap.go:192-196`); matching is by **longest path prefix** via `SurfaceFor` (`keymap.go:226-238`). Two entries only: `o` on `security/results/ci-tab`, and `ctrl+y` on `oci/launch-form`. Accessors: `DeclaredExceptions()` `:270-272`, `IsException(key)` `:275-282`.

## 5. `internal/ui/shared` → actually **`internal/shared`**

There is no `internal/ui/shared`. The package is **`/c/.../internal/shared/state.go`**, `package shared`, type `State` at `:56-108`:

- `Secrets credentials.Selection` + `SecretNotices []string` (`:61-62`) — resolved once per context by the router; **must be reused**, a second `credentials.Select()` yields a fresh `MemoryStorage`.
- `Forge forge.Forge`, `IsAuthenticated bool`, `CurrentUser forge.User` (`:72-77`).
- Dashboard data: `ServiceStatus`, `ServiceComponents`, `ForgeStats`, `DockerStats`, `OCIStats`, `WorkspaceCount`, `Tools` (`:98-107`).

**What a view actually receives is decided per-case in `createView`** (`internal/app/command_line.go:168-200`) — there is no uniform signature:

| Shape | Views |
|---|---|
| `New(a.config, a.sharedState)` | dashboard, git-explorer |
| `New(a.config)` | status, containers, oci-resources, netdiag, viewer, about |
| `New(a.config, a.sharedState.Secrets.Storage)` | workspaces, security, templates |

## 6. Cross-view navigation — the `OriginView` mechanism

Three views implement it identically. The pattern has **four parts**:

**(a) The producer emits an open request.** It names only what it knows — never itself:
- `internal/ui/status/update.go:207` → `netdiag.OpenRequestMsg{Target, AutoRun}`

# §3.1 — Redirecteur de ports non privilégié (4e onglet de `:net`) > À recopier dans `.claude/plans/port-forward-plan.md` au début de > l'implémentation (règle de `.claude/rules/planning.md`). ## Contexte §3.1 du backlog tient en une ligne depuis `todo.md` : « *Port-forwarding manager — an interactive dashboard to manage port redirections to the host machine* ». L'analyse qui précède ce plan a tranché deux choses : 1. **Les alias de noms via `/etc/hosts` sont abandonnés.** Ils demandent une élévation sur les trois plateformes (UAC sous Windows même pour un compte administrateur), trois mécanismes distincts, et une réinvocation auto-élevée qui est une surface d'élévation de privilèges à sécuriser. Cela irait aussi à l'encontre de §3.43/§3.44, qui ont retiré le dernier conteneur privilégié de l'application. 2. **Le redirecteur, lui, ne demande aucun droit.** C'est un `net.Listen` + deux `io.Copy` dans le process DevDesk. Mesuré dans le sandbox Linux : bind refusé sur 80 et 443 en non-root, accepté sur 8080. Windows n'a pas de plage réservée. Se limiter aux ports ≥ 1024 rend la fonctionnalité portable sans privilège. Résultat visé : depuis `:net`, ouvrir un port local vers un `host:port` quelconque — avec pré-remplissage depuis un conteneur en cours d'exécution et ses ports **non publiés**, qui est le cas d'usage qui a le plus de valeur (joindre un service sans redémarrer le conteneur). ## Décisions déjà prises | Question | Réponse | |---|---| | Cible | Proxy TCP générique + pré-remplissage depuis un conteneur | | Persistance | **Session seulement** — rien dans le YAML, aucune migration | | Emplacement | **4e onglet de `:net`**, à côté de Diagnostics / Ports / Interfaces | La persistance session-seulement n'est pas qu'une simplification : un listener ne peut pas survivre au process qui le détient, donc une liste persistée promettrait ce qu'elle ne peut pas tenir. ## Le risque principal — à mesurer AVANT d'écrire le pré-remplissage conteneur **C'est une rechute possible de D55.** `docs/architecture/network.md:181-191` raconte que l'onglet Ports listait les sockets de la VM Docker Desktop en croyant parler de l'hôte, et que `K` tuait un process de la VM. Le mécanisme est le même ici : sous Docker Desktop (Windows, macOS), **l'IP d'un conteneur n'est pas routable depuis l'hôte** — elle l'est sous Docker natif Linux. Un redirecteur qui composerait `172.17.0.2:80` marcherait sur la machine du développeur Linux et échouerait sur celle de l'utilisateur. Deux mesures à faire sur l'**hôte Windows**, avant l'étape 3 : 1. Lancer un conteneur avec un port exposé non publié, lire son IP (`docker inspect`), et tenter un `Test-NetConnection -Port

` depuis l'hôte. C'est la mesure qui décide. 2. Vérifier que `docker inspect` et `podman inspect` s'accordent sur `.NetworkSettings.Networks.*.IPAddress` — même classe de divergence que les trois gabarits trouvés en §3.67. **Ce que le plan fait de ce risque, quelle qu'en soit l'issue** : le redirecteur **sonde** la cible avant d'ouvrir le listener, et rapporte l'échec en nommant la cause probable. Il ne détecte pas la plateforme et ne devine rien — c'est la philosophie de `netcheck` (mesurer, pas supposer), et c'est ce qui empêche un « ça marche chez moi » silencieux. ## Architecture ### Qui détient les listeners — le routeur, jamais la vue `internal/app/app.go:343` : `reinitializeViews` fait `a.views = make(map[...])` à chaque sauvegarde de config et à chaque changement de contexte. **Un listener détenu par le modèle netdiag fuirait à ce moment-là**, sans que rien ne le signale. Le précédent exact est le serveur MCP (`internal/app/mcp.go`) : `net.Listen` dans un `Cmd` (l'I/O appartient au `Cmd`, Rule 110), le handle revient **sur un message**, et `Update` est le seul à le stocker. `sharedState` est créé une fois dans `newWithSize` (`app.go:205`) et muté sur place — il survit donc aux reconstructions de vues. Le modèle à suivre est celui de `internal/jobs`, qui est le plus proche : le routeur détient le registre (`a.jobs = jobs.New()`, `app.go:216`), les vues ne le reçoivent **pas** ; elles émettent un message de demande et reçoivent un **instantané** en retour (`jobs.StartMsg` → `handleStartJobs` → `jobs.ChangedMsg`, `internal/app/jobs.go:18-58`). Les types de messages vivent dans le paquet du domaine, pas dans `internal/app`, pour que les vues puissent les importer sans importer le routeur. ### Nouveau paquet `internal/forward` Aucune dépendance à `internal/docker` ni à l'UI — il ne connaît que des `host:port`. C'est ce qui le rend testable sans conteneur. ```go // Forward is one live redirection, as the table reads it. type Forward struct { ID string // stable across snapshots; the datatable Key LocalPort int Target string // host:port Label string // where it came from: a container name, or empty Opened time.Time Active int // connections currently proxied Total int64 // connections accepted since it opened LastErr string // last dial failure, empty when healthy } type Registry struct { /* mu sync.Mutex; entries map[string]*entry */ } func New() *Registry func (r *Registry) Open(localPort int, target, label string) (Forward, error) func (r *Registry) Close(id string) error func (r *Registry) CloseAll() func (r *Registry) List() []Forward // sorted snapshot, safe to hand to a view ``` Quatre décisions à écrire dans le code, chacune avec son test : - **`Open` écoute sur `127.0.0.1` uniquement, jamais `0.0.0.0`.** Publier sur toutes les interfaces exposerait au LAN un service que le conteneur avait justement gardé pour lui — c'est exactement ce que §3.64 cherche à repérer, et le faire ici par défaut serait contradictoire. Pas d'option pour l'instant. - **Les ports < 1024 sont refusés avant l'appel système**, avec une raison nommée, plutôt que de laisser remonter un `bind: permission denied` qui ne dit pas que la limite est structurelle et sans contournement non privilégié. - **La cible est sondée avant que le listener n'ouvre.** Un `net.DialTimeout` court : ça échoue tout de suite et clairement, plutôt qu'à la première connexion, une fois que l'utilisateur a déjà pointé son client dessus. C'est aussi ce qui attrape le cas Docker Desktop décrit plus haut. - **Les compteurs sont atomiques** — ils sont écrits par les goroutines de connexion et lus par `List()` depuis `Update`. `mise run test-race` est la vérification qui compte ici. Boucle d'accept dans une goroutine, une goroutine par connexion, deux `io.Copy` à contre-sens, `ln.Close()` termine l'accept (l'erreur attendue est `net.ErrClosed` — même distinction que `http.ErrServerClosed` dans `mcp.go:107`). ### Câblage routeur | | | |---|---| | `internal/shared/state.go` | + `Forwards *forward.Registry` (créé une fois, comme `jobs`) | | `internal/app/app.go` | construire le registre dans `newWithSize` | | `internal/app/forward.go` (nouveau) | `handleForwardOpen` / `handleForwardClose` / `forwardsChanged()`, calqués sur `internal/app/jobs.go` | | `internal/app/app.go` `Update` | router `forward.OpenMsg` et `forward.CloseMsg` | | `internal/app/command_line.go:186` | `netdiag.New(a.config)` reçoit le registre, ou plutôt : la vue n'a besoin de rien — elle reçoit `forward.ChangedMsg` | **Les redirections survivent au changement de contexte** — contrairement au serveur MCP, qui redémarre parce qu'il répond *pour* un contexte. Une redirection est un port local vers un `host:port` ; elle n'appartient à aucun contexte. À écrire comme une décision, pas la subir. Rien à faire à la fermeture : `tea.Quit` sort du process et l'OS reprend les ports (`keys.go:42`, le serveur MCP ne fait rien de plus). ### L'onglet `internal/ui/netdiag/forward_model.go` + `forward_view.go`, sur le modèle exact de `ports_model.go` — une `datatable.Model[forward.Forward]`, pas de `FilterBar` locale (elle appartient au datatable via `Config.Tokens`). Colonnes (chacune déclare son `Sizing`, Rule 116/§3.45) : | Titre | Sizing | Note | |---|---|---| | `Local` | Fixed | le port local | | `Target` | Content | `host:port` | | `Source` | Content | le nom du conteneur, ou `-` en `DimStyle` | | `Conns` | Fixed | actives / total ; un `0` en `DimStyle` (Rule 122) | | `Age` | Fixed | `theme.TimeAgo(f.Opened)` (Rule 127) | | `State` | Fixed | `StatusColumn` — la cellule que le spinner occupe | Touches — **aucune lettre nouvelle n'est nécessaire**, ce qui est le bon signe : - `N` (`keymap.New`, « Create a resource from this context ») ouvre le formulaire. - `K` (`keymap.Kill`, « Stop, kill ») ferme la redirection sélectionnée, via `components.ConfirmModal` comme le kill de l'onglet Ports. - `/` cherche. **Pas de toggle minuscule** au premier jet : `localToggles` (`internal/ui/keymap/keymap.go:206-217`) fait correspondre les fichiers par préfixe, et `ui/netdiag/` n'autorise que `p` — un `forward_model.go` qui binderait une minuscule devrait donc déclarer sa propre surface. Inutile pour une table de quelques lignes. Ajouter un 4e onglet demande de toucher **trois** endroits, et le `% 3` est le piège : - `model.go:31-35` — `tabForward = 3`, et y ajouter un `tabCount = 4` plutôt que de laisser deux littéraux `3` se balader. - `update.go:153-160` — les deux `% 3` deviennent `% tabCount`. - `header.go:204-209` — la 4e `theme.TabItem{Label: "Forward"}`. Puis les branches par onglet, toutes dans les mêmes fonctions que Ports : `View` (`view.go:19-34`), `GetShortcuts` / `GetHeaderInfo` / `GetFooterHeight` / `RenderFooter` / `activeFooter` (`header.go`), `InEditMode` (`update.go:22-39`), `resize` et le routage des messages (`update.go:59`, `:71-75`, `:163-167`). `GetHelpContent` (`header.go:242`) gagne sa section. **À corriger au passage** : la `Description` et la première entrée de `KeyBindings` disent encore « Topology » là où le reste du fichier dit « Interfaces ». ### Le formulaire `internal/ui/netdiag/forward_form.go`, calqué sur `internal/ui/oci_resources/launch_form.go` — `textinput` + `theme.StyleTextInput`, navigation `↑↓` (Rule 103/135), `enter` valide, `esc` annule, une ligne vide en tête (Rule 131), et **aucune ligne d'aide dans le viewport** (Rule 134). Trois champs : port local, cible (`host:port`), et un champ conteneur en cycle `←→` (Rule 132) qui, quand il n'est pas vide, **remplit** la cible plutôt que de la remplacer par un mode à part — un seul chemin d'exécution, le conteneur n'est qu'une façon de remplir le formulaire. Le pré-remplissage lit `docker.ListContainers(false)` et ne propose que les `PortBinding` de scope `docker.ScopeExposed` — `container_ports.go:16-18` les définit comme « *a port the image declares and nothing published… there is no host port to connect to* », c'est-à-dire exactement la population qui a besoin d'une redirection. L'IP vient de `docker.InspectContainer` (JSON complet, `containers.go:310`) ; si les deux moteurs divergent sur ce champ (mesure 2 ci-dessus), ça devient un champ de `engine.Templates`. ### Disponibilité (Rule 130) `internal/ui/netdiag/forward_model.go`, sur le modèle mince de `ports_model.go:472-493` (constantes nommées + une méthode rendant `shortcut.Availability`, refus explicite au footer en `Warn`) : - `reasonNoForwardRow` — `K` sur une table vide. - `reasonPortPrivileged` — un port < 1024 saisi. - `reasonPortTaken` — le bind a été refusé ; c'est un `Error` au sens de Rule 128 (le système a dit non), pas un `Warn`. - `reasonTargetUnreachable` — la sonde a échoué. Le message nomme la cause probable quand la cible est une IP de conteneur. ## Découpage 1. **`internal/forward` seul**, avec ses tests. Aucune UI, aucun docker : un listener, un proxy, un registre. C'est la moitié qui porte le risque de race et elle se teste entièrement en mémoire. 2. **Le câblage routeur** — `shared.State`, `internal/app/forward.go`, le routage des deux messages. Toujours pas d'écran. 3. **L'onglet et le formulaire**, cible saisie à la main. À ce stade la fonctionnalité est complète et portable. 4. **Le pré-remplissage conteneur**, après les deux mesures. C'est la seule étape qui peut se révéler inutile sous Docker Desktop, et la mettre en dernier est ce qui empêche qu'elle entraîne les trois autres. ## Vérification ```bash go build ./... go test ./internal/forward/ ./internal/ui/netdiag/ ./internal/app/ mise run test-race # celui qui compte : goroutines + compteurs mise run lint ``` Tests à écrire, au-delà de la couverture ordinaire : - un aller-retour complet sur `127.0.0.1` (echo server en mémoire) ; - `Close` pendant qu'une connexion est ouverte ; - le refus d'un port < 1024 **sans** appel système ; - le refus d'un port déjà pris ; - `TestShortcutKeys` pour l'onglet : le jeu de touches ne change pas d'un état à l'autre du même écran (Rule 130) ; - Rule 116 : `RenderedWidth() == width-2` sur la nouvelle table. Bout en bout, **depuis l'hôte** (le sandbox n'est pas représentatif : pas de vrai terminal, pas le Docker de l'hôte) : lancer un conteneur avec un port exposé non publié, ouvrir une redirection dessus, et vérifier avec un client. C'est aussi la mesure 1 du risque D55. ## Documentation à mettre à jour dans le même commit - `docs/architecture/network.md` — une section après « The socket table », qui dit surtout pourquoi le listener appartient au routeur et pourquoi il écoute sur loopback. - `docs/backlog.md` §3.1 — remplacer la ligne héritée de `todo.md` par l'entrée réelle : les alias `hosts` écartés avec leur raison, la contrainte ≥ 1024, et ce que la mesure D55 aura donné. - `.claude/CLAUDE.md` — la ligne « Network diagnostics » de l'aperçu projet.

## A5. **CRITICAL — long-lived background goroutines**

### Yes, exactly one, and it is the MCP HTTP server.

`/…/internal/app/mcp.go`. This is your closest precedent for a TCP forwarder, and it is a very close one — it opens a `net.Listen("tcp", …)` and keeps serving.

```go
ln, err := net.Listen("tcp", addr)          // mcp.go:95   (inside the Cmd — I/O belongs in a Cmd)
srv := &http.Server{Handler: handler}       // 100
go func() {                                 // 101 — the long-lived goroutine
    if err := srv.Serve(ln); err != nil && !errors.Is(err, http.ErrServerClosed) {
        log.Printf("ERROR [app/mcp] serve: %v", err)
    }
}()
return MCPServerStartedMsg{Epoch: epoch, Addr: ln.Addr().String(), Server: srv, Token: token}  // 112
```

Lifecycle management, in full:

- **Handle stored in the model, never in the Cmd**: `mcpServer *http.Server` at `/…/internal/app/app.go:114` (alongside `mcpAddr`, `mcpErr`, `mcpToken`, `mcpEpoch`, `program`, `mcpDispatch`). Stored only by `handleMCPServerStarted` (`mcp.go:166`), i.e. from `Update`.
- **Start**: `Init()` batches `a.startMCPCmd()` (`/…/internal/app/app.go:262`).
- **The thing created in the Cmd travels back on a message** — `mcp.go:54-57` states this explicitly: *"The listener is opened here, inside the Cmd, and handed back on the message. That is the same shape as a scan's `context.CancelFunc` travelling on its starting message: the thing is created where the I/O happens and stored by the one place allowed to store it."*
- **Epoch guard against races**: `MCPServerStartedMsg.Epoch` (`mcp.go:31`), incremented in `startMCPCmd` (59-60). A report from a superseded start has its listener **closed on arrival rather than stored** (`mcp.go:171-177`). Without this a slow start (keyring unlock, `git config`) could store a listener for a context the user has left.
- **Stop/restart on context switch**: `restartMCPCmd` (`mcp.go:135`) clears the four fields, then `tea.Sequence(close-the-old, start-the-new)` using `srv.Close()` (not `Shutdown` — an in-flight request belongs to the context being left, line 148-152). Called from `handleContextSwitchComplete`: `/…/internal/app/context.go:190` — `tea.Batch(a.requestResize(), initCmd, a.jobsChanged(), a.restartMCPCmd())`.
- **Cleanup on quit: there is none, and that is deliberate/implicit.** `q` and `ctrl+c` return bare `tea.Quit` (`/…/internal/app/keys.go:42`, `129`; `command_line.go:70`). `main.go` has no teardown beyond `defer logFile.Close()` (`main.go:72`). The server dies with the process. **If your forwarder has state to flush or a socket peer to notify, there is no existing quit hook — you would be the first to need one.**
- **The goroutine → `Update` door**: `/…/internal/app/invoke.go:16-33` documents it as *"exactly one legal way across: `tea.Program.Send`, and then `Update()` replies (Rule 110)"*. The handle is written once by `AttachProgram` in `main.go:105`, **before `p.Run()`**. The adapter is a value type (`mcpDispatcher`, `invoke.go:43`) holding only the program handle *"so it must be unable to reach a field of the model even by accident"*. Reply channels are **buffered to one** so `Update` can never block on a client that hung up.

```go
func waitForCloneEvent(events <-chan cloneEvent) tea.Cmd {                     // 212
```

`templates/scan.go:114`, `templates/sync.go:70`, `workspaces/commands.go:170`, `oci_resources/commands.go:114` & `589`, `security/inventory_commands.go:239`, `scan/run.go:108`, `ports/resolve.go:87` — all created inside a Cmd and released by `defer cancel()`; only the `CancelFunc` escapes, on the starting message, into `Registry.advance`.

**Summary for your forwarder**: the MCP server is the only precedent for a process-lifetime listener, and it gives you the whole recipe — open the listener in a Cmd, hand the `*net.Listener`/closer back on a message, store it in the App model, guard concurrent starts with an epoch counter, restart on context switch via `tea.Sequence(close, start)`, and push events from the accept goroutine through `p.Send` (or a buffered channel + a re-issued `waitFor…` Cmd, à la the clone pipeline). ## B4. The migration mechanism

`applyDefaults` (`config.go:400`) is the single entry point, called by `LoadContext` (`config.go:754`) before path expansion. Ordering is load-bearing and documented at 403-412:

```go

// would find a block that is no longer empty and take the field-by-field
// path — where every field is already filled with a default, and the user's
// own `parallel_jobs: 7` is silently dropped. Measured, not theorised …
// The other half of the reason is `docker:` → `network:`'s: yaml.Unmarshal
// is not strict here, so an un-migrated block is dropped in silence, and the
// silence would point a context at no host at all.

```

```go
	Invocation string                // MCP call id, empty for a keypress (§3.61)
}
func Start(run Run, work tea.Cmd) tea.Cmd                                       // 106
func StartInContext(run Run, work func(contextName string) tea.Cmd) tea.Cmd     // 168
func StartCancellable(run Run, work tea.Cmd, cancel context.CancelFunc) tea.Cmd // 113
func WithInvocation(invocation string, cmd tea.Cmd) tea.Cmd                     // 64
func Cancel(id JobID) tea.Cmd / CancelItem(id, target) / CancelOpen(kind)       // 149/160/134
type ChangedMsg struct { Runs []Run; Frame string; RenderedFrame string }       // 184
```

The flow, all in `Update`:

1. View returns `jobs.Start(run, cmd)` → a `StartMsg`.
2. Router `handleStartJobs` (`/…/internal/app/jobs.go:40`) stamps `run.Context = a.currentContext`, calls `a.jobs.Start(run)`, attaches the run-level cancel, then **dispatches the work after registration** — `message.go:16-21` explains why the work rides on the message rather than a `tea.Batch`: "a transition naming a run the registry has not admitted yet is refused, and a tea.Batch gives no order."
3. The Cmd emits a *starting* message then a *complete* message (`tea.Sequence`), each implementing `Reporter`.
4. Router `routeWork` (`/…/internal/app/jobs.go:70`) applies the transition to the registry **before** forwarding the message to the owning view, then broadcasts.
5. `broadcastJobs` (`jobs.go:185`) pushes a `jobs.ChangedMsg` into **every** held view (on screen or not), then re-measures layout once.

A context cancel is created *inside* the Cmd and travels on the starting message so the registry stores it in the same `Update` that marks the item running — no window where a row runs but can't be stopped (`registry.go:71-77`, `templates/scan.go:54-61`).

## A3. `:jobs` view and the single spinner chain

**View**: `/…/internal/ui/jobsview/` — `model.go` (tables/columns), `update.go` (message + keys), `view.go` (header/footer/help), `state.go`, `availability.go`.

- Owns nothing, fetches nothing: `Init()` returns `nil` (`update.go:17`). Rows come only from `jobs.ChangedMsg` → `handleJobsChanged` (`update.go:42`) → `refreshRows()` (73) rebuilding **both** tables.
- Two levels (`levelRuns` / `levelItems`, `model.go:28-33`), `→` drills, `esc`/`←` goes up.
- `K` (`keymap.Kill`) → `stopSelected` (`update.go:144`) emits `jobs.Cancel(row.Run.ID)` or `jobs.CancelItem(m.openRun, target)` — it asks, never writes the registry.
- Filters to the current context: `visibleRuns()` = `jobs.FilterContext(m.runs, m.contextName)` (`update.go:52`).

**Spinner chain** — `/…/internal/app/jobs.go:127-245`. One chain for the whole app (D5):

```go
type jobTickMsg struct{ seq int }                       // 133 — router's own type, not spinner.TickMsg
var jobSpinnerInterval = spinner.Dot.FPS                // 148 (var, so testutil.FastTimers can shorten it)
func (a *App) jobsChanged() tea.Cmd { return tea.Batch(a.broadcastJobs(), a.ensureJobTick()) }  // 169
func (a *App) ensureJobTick() tea.Cmd                   // 218 — the ONLY place a chain starts
func (a *App) handleJobTick(msg jobTickMsg) (...)       // 235 — stops by not renewing
```

`ensureJobTick` no-ops if `a.jobTicking` or `a.jobs.Running() == 0`; `jobTickSeq` invalidates ticks from an older chain. `changedMsg()` (line 18) fills `Frame` (bare — Rule 122, table cells are measured before styling) and `RenderedFrame` (styled — Rule 128, for footers). App fields: `jobs`, `jobFrameIdx`, `jobTickSeq`, `jobTicking` at `/…/internal/app/app.go:92-99`.

The shared footer line: `/…/internal/ui/components/jobs_status.go:35` `JobsStatusLine(runs []jobs.Run, origin command.ViewType) string` — three forms, degrading to `"3 jobs running — :jobs for details"`.

## A4. End-to-end trace — template sync (`/…/internal/ui/templates/sync.go`)

1. **Key press** → `startSync()` (line 95). Guard `m.availability().Sync` (built on `syncState()`, line 87, which asks the registry via `m.working(jobs.KindSync, slug)`). Everything the Cmd needs is read here into a `syncJob` (59) — Rule 110.
2. **Register + dispatch**: `return m, jobs.Start(run, syncTemplateCmd(job))` with `run := jobs.NewRun(jobs.KindSync, command.ViewTemplates, "", entry.Name, entry.Slug)` (105-106).
3. **Router**: `app.Update` case `jobs.StartMsg` (`/…/internal/app/app.go:~455`) → `handleStartJobs` registers, then runs `msg.Work(run.Context)`.
4. **Cmd**: `syncTemplateCmd` (65) = `tea.Sequence(SyncStartingMsg → SyncCompleteMsg)`; the I/O uses its own `context.WithTimeout(…, syncTimeout)` created *inside* the Cmd (70).
5. **Messages back**: both implement `Reporter` — `SyncStartingMsg.Transition()` (39) → `ItemRunning`; `SyncCompleteMsg.Transition()` (43) → `ItemDone` or `ItemFailed` with `Detail: "sync failed — check logs"`. Compile-time proof at lines 52-55.
6. **Routing**: `app.Update` → `routeWork(command.ViewTemplates, msg)` → `Registry.Apply` (which resolves the run via `FindItem(kind, target)` — views never hold a `JobID`) → `jobsChanged()` → broadcast + ensure tick.
7. **Completion**: view's `handleSyncComplete` (110) prints the footer line; `Run.Finished()` becomes true when every item is terminal, `settle()` stamps `EndedAt`, `Running()` hits 0 and `handleJobTick` lets the chain die.

The scan variant (`/…/internal/ui/templates/scan.go:112` `scanTemplateCmd`, `199` `startScan`) is the same but uses `jobs.StartInContext` so `contextName` is stamped once and carried into the cache write (D68), and its starting message carries `Cancel` (line 76).

## A5. **CRITICAL — long-lived background goroutines**

### Yes, exactly one, and it is the MCP HTTP server.

`/…/internal/app/mcp.go`. This is your closest precedent for a TCP forwarder, and it is a very close one — it opens a `net.Listen("tcp", …)` and keeps serving.

```go
ln, err := net.Listen("tcp", addr)          // mcp.go:95   (inside the Cmd — I/O belongs in a Cmd)
srv := &http.Server{Handler: handler}       // 100
go func() {                                 // 101 — the long-lived goroutine
    if err := srv.Serve(ln); err != nil && !errors.Is(err, http.ErrServerClosed) {
        log.Printf("ERROR [app/mcp] serve: %v", err)
    }
}()
return MCPServerStartedMsg{Epoch: epoch, Addr: ln.Addr().String(), Server: srv, Token: token}  // 112
```

Lifecycle management, in full:

- **Handle stored in the model, never in the Cmd**: `mcpServer *http.Server` at `/…/internal/app/app.go:114` (alongside `mcpAddr`, `mcpErr`, `mcpToken`, `mcpEpoch`, `program`, `mcpDispatch`). Stored only by `handleMCPServerStarted` (`mcp.go:166`), i.e. from `Update`.
- **Start**: `Init()` batches `a.startMCPCmd()` (`/…/internal/app/app.go:262`).
- **The thing created in the Cmd travels back on a message** — `mcp.go:54-57` states this explicitly: *"The listener is opened here, inside the Cmd, and handed back on the message. That is the same shape as a scan's `context.CancelFunc` travelling on its starting message: the thing is created where the I/O happens and stored by the one place allowed to store it."*
- **Epoch guard against races**: `MCPServerStartedMsg.Epoch` (`mcp.go:31`), incremented in `startMCPCmd` (59-60). A report from a superseded start has its listener **closed on arrival rather than stored** (`mcp.go:171-177`). Without this a slow start (keyring unlock, `git config`) could store a listener for a context the user has left.
- **Stop/restart on context switch**: `restartMCPCmd` (`mcp.go:135`) clears the four fields, then `tea.Sequence(close-the-old, start-the-new)` using `srv.Close()` (not `Shutdown` — an in-flight request belongs to the context being left, line 148-152). Called from `handleContextSwitchComplete`: `/…/internal/app/context.go:190` — `tea.Batch(a.requestResize(), initCmd, a.jobsChanged(), a.restartMCPCmd())`.
- **Cleanup on quit: there is none, and that is deliberate/implicit.** `q` and `ctrl+c` return bare `tea.Quit` (`/…/internal/app/keys.go:42`, `129`; `command_line.go:70`). `main.go` has no teardown beyond `defer logFile.Close()` (`main.go:72`). The server dies with the process. **If your forwarder has state to flush or a socket peer to notify, there is no existing quit hook — you would be the first to need one.**
- **The goroutine → `Update` door**: `/…/internal/app/invoke.go:16-33` documents it as *"exactly one legal way across: `tea.Program.Send`, and then `Update()` replies (Rule 110)"*. The handle is written once by `AttachProgram` in `main.go:105`, **before `p.Run()`**. The adapter is a value type (`mcpDispatcher`, `invoke.go:43`) holding only the program handle *"so it must be unable to reach a field of the model even by accident"*. Reply channels are **buffered to one** so `Update` can never block on a client that hung up.

### The second pattern: a pipeline goroutine + channel + re-issued read Cmd

`/…/internal/ui/forge/explorer/pipeline.go` — the clone. This is the pattern to copy if the forwarder emits a stream of events (connection opened/closed/bytes):

```go
type cloneRun struct { events <-chan cloneEvent; cancel context.CancelFunc }   // 92
func startCloneRun(spec cloneSpec) *cloneRun {                                 // 103
	ctx, cancel := context.WithCancel(context.Background())
	events := make(chan cloneEvent, cloneEventBuffer)   // buffered 256, line 56 — keeps workers off the UI critical path
	go runPipeline(ctx, spec, events)
	return &cloneRun{events: events, cancel: cancel}
}
func waitForCloneEvent(events <-chan cloneEvent) tea.Cmd {                     // 212
	return func() tea.Msg {
		event, ok := <-events
		if !ok { return CloneRunFinishedMsg{} }   // closed channel = the run is over
		return CloneEventMsg{event: event}
	}
}
```

`runPipeline` does `defer close(events)` (112) and **drains rather than abandons** the inner channel on cancel (146-153): *"a goroutine holding a live HTTP client is a leak that outlives the view."*

Started **from `Update`** so the cancel exists before registration — `/…/internal/ui/forge/explorer/clone.go:102-125`:

```go
run := startCloneRun(cloneSpec{…})
m.clone = newCloneList(msg.Path, run.events)      // the channel lives in the model
return m, tea.Batch(
	jobs.StartCancellable(m.cloneJobRun(msg.Path), waitForCloneEvent(run.events), run.cancel),
	m.spinner.Tick,
)
```

Cancel goes *through the registry*, never around it — `handleCloneEsc` (`clone.go:227`) returns `jobs.CancelOpen(jobs.KindClone)`, with the reasoning at 239-242: *"Calling the pipeline's cancel from here would stop the walk behind the registry's back, and leave the record claiming the run finished on its own."* Each event handler re-issues the read (`clone.go:162`). Model-held channel: `/…/internal/ui/forge/explorer/clone_list.go:54-56`.

### The third pattern: self-rearming `tea.Tick` loops guarded by a generation counter

No `time.Ticker` anywhere — only `tea.Tick` chains:

- `/…/internal/ui/viewer/update.go:41-50` + `model.go:75-81`: `followTickMsg{gen int}` + `m.followGen`; `startFollowing` increments the gen (`update.go:359`), `stopFollowing` (366) is *"the one place following is turned off, so no path can leave the flag set with no tick behind it, or a tick running with the flag clear."* A non-positive interval is refused (44-49).
- `/…/internal/app/jobs.go:133-154`: the same shape with `seq`.
- `/…/internal/ui/dashboard/model.go:633, 647, 697`: three independent clocks; `refreshAll` *"only rearms its own clock"* (line ~705) to avoid doubling the rate.
- `/…/internal/ui/netdiag/ports_model.go:48-60`, `/…/internal/ui/status/commands.go:14`, `/…/internal/ui/oci_resources/commands.go:45`, `/…/internal/ui/containers/commands.go:15`.

### Everything else with `go func()` or `context.WithCancel` is scoped to one Cmd

`templates/scan.go:114`, `templates/sync.go:70`, `workspaces/commands.go:170`, `oci_resources/commands.go:114` & `589`, `security/inventory_commands.go:239`, `scan/run.go:108`, `ports/resolve.go:87` — all created inside a Cmd and released by `defer cancel()`; only the `CancelFunc` escapes, on the starting message, into `Registry.advance`.

**Summary for your forwarder**: the MCP server is the only precedent for a process-lifetime listener, and it gives you the whole recipe — open the listener in a Cmd, hand the `*net.Listener`/closer back on a message, store it in the App model, guard concurrent starts with an epoch counter, restart on context switch via `tea.Sequence(close, start)`, and push events from the accept goroutine through `p.Send` (or a buffered channel + a re-issued `waitFor…` Cmd, à la the clone pipeline). The registry gives you rows, a spinner and a `K` key for free if you model connections as `Item`s of an **open** run (`NewOpenRun` + `Discover` + `Seal`) — but note `Kind.Cancellable()` (`jobs.go:63`) currently whitelists only scan and pull, and `Kinds()` (41) is walked by a test that will fail for a new kind without an icon and a verb.

## B1. The `Config` struct

`/…/internal/config/config.go:14-28`:

```go

	App      AppConfig      `yaml:"app"`
	Status   StatusConfig   `yaml:"status"`
	Forge    ForgeConfig    `yaml:"forge"`

	Scan     ScanConfig     `yaml:"scan"`

	GitLab GitLabConfig `yaml:"gitlab,omitempty"`

```

**`app:`** — `AppConfig` at line 135: `theme, log_file, default_view, workspaces_dir, ide_command, terminal_command, terminal_new_window, show_hidden_files, secret_backend, container_engine`. Note 165-171 on `ContainerEngine`: it sits in `app` because *"this section already holds the external tools the application drives — and deliberately not in `network`, which carries only netcheck's dials despite once being called `docker` (§3.67)."* That sentence is the governing precedent for where a forwarder's settings belong.

**`network:`** — `NetworkConfig` at line 100, deliberately thin:

```go

	CheckTimeout         int `yaml:"check_timeout"`
	PingCount            int `yaml:"ping_count"`
```

## B2. Lists of structs in a context YAML

Two existing examples.

**Registries** (the richer one): `RegistryConfig.Registries []RegistryItem \`yaml:"registries,omitempty"\`` (`config.go:287`); `RegistryItem` at 228 with `slug`, `kind`, `parent`, `provider`, `url`, `username`, `alias`, `repo_prefix`, `auth_mode`, deprecated `auth_enabled`, `management_url`. ```go

which fills missing slugs (`ProposeSlug`/`uniqueSlug`), migrates the deprecated bool (`applyAuthMode`, 198), and refuses bad input (`checkParents`, `checkRepoPrefixes` at 177, `checkAuthModes`). It is called **last** in `applyDefaults` (`config.go:533`) and its error aborts the load (`LoadContext` wraps it as `invalid context '%s'`, `config.go:757`).

Writing side: `/…/internal/ui/oci_resources/registries.go:149-160` — `handleRegistryFormSubmit` appends or replaces in `m.config.Registry.Registries`, refreshes the table, then `config.Save(m.config)` and reports via footer. A form submit message carries the whole `config.RegistryItem`.

**Status monitors** (the simpler one): `StatusConfig.Components []ComponentConfig \`yaml:"components"\`` (`config.go:352-374`); `ComponentConfig` has `name, type, target, timeout, url (deprecated), count, nameserver`. Persisted by `/…/internal/ui/status/commands.go:40-61` — two Cmds that do **only** the write:

```go

func saveComponent(cfg *config.Config) tea.Cmd {
	return func() tea.Msg {
		err := config.Save(cfg)
```

The model mutation happens in `Update`; the Cmd only writes and returns an outcome message.

## B3. `config.Save()` and its callers

```go
func Save(cfg *Config) error {                    // config.go:616
	ctx, err := GetCurrentContext()
	if err != nil { ctx = "default" }
	return SaveContext(cfg, ctx)
}
func SaveContext(cfg *Config, contextName string) error {  // config.go:813
	// ValidateContextName → GetContextPath → EnsureConfigDir → yaml.Marshal → os.WriteFile(path, data, 0600)
}
```

Paths: `~/.devdesk/config.yaml` for `default`, `~/.devdesk/config-<name>.yaml` otherwise (`GetContextPath`, 863; `LoadContext` doc at 727-729). Current context from `~/.devdesk/.current-context` (`GetCurrentContext`, 630; `CurrentContextName`, 663). Mode `0600`.

Note the asymmetry: `Save` does **not** re-run `applyDefaults`, so deprecated fields cleared at load (`cfg.GitLab = GitLabConfig{}`, `item.AuthEnabled = false`) disappear from the file on the next save — that is the documented migration-retirement mechanism.

Non-test callers of `config.Save`:
- `/…/internal/ui/configuration/update.go:326` (`persist`, the main config screen) and `:363` (`handleBackendConfirmed`)
- `/…/internal/ui/oci_resources/registries.go:160` (registry form submit)
- `/…/internal/ui/oci_resources/results.go:58`
- `/…/internal/ui/status/commands.go:43` and `:55`
- `/…/internal/app/forge.go:79`
- `config.SaveContext` directly: `/…/internal/ui/setup/commands.go:115`

`persist` (`configuration/update.go:323-341`) is the pattern: apply cross-field constraints → `config.Save` → return `ConfigSavedMsg{Config, ThemeChanged, ForgeChanged, EngineChanged}`; the router handles it at `app.Update` case `configuration.ConfigSavedMsg` → `handleConfigSaved`. The `saved` struct (309-321) is how a save tells the router "this one needs an action, not just a rebuild" — that is where a forwarder restart-on-save would hook in, exactly like `engineChanged`.

## B4. The migration mechanism

`applyDefaults` (`config.go:400`) is the single entry point, called by `LoadContext` (`config.go:754`) before path expansion. Ordering is load-bearing and documented at 403-412:

```go
// `gitlab:` → `forge:`, and it runs **first**. That is not tidiness: every
// default below writes into cfg.Forge, so a migration placed after them
// would find a block that is no longer empty and take the field-by-field
// path — where every field is already filled with a default, and the user's
// own `parallel_jobs: 7` is silently dropped. Measured, not theorised …
// The other half of the reason is `docker:` → `network:`'s: yaml.Unmarshal
// is not strict here, so an un-migrated block is dropped in silence, and the
// silence would point a context at no host at all.
migrateGitLabSection(cfg)
```

`migrateGitLabSection` — `/…/internal/config/forge.go:32-81`. Its shape is the template for any new section:

1. Early-return if the legacy struct is the zero value (34).
2. `defer` that fills the new discriminator and **clears the legacy struct** so the key leaves the file on the next save (37-44).
3. Whole-block copy when the new section is entirely absent (49-61) — *"the only case where a bool can be carried over safely: `IncludeArchived`'s zero value *is* false, so no per-field guard could tell 'unset' from 'deliberately off'."*
4. Field-by-field, new-wins otherwise, for hand-edited files carrying both (66-80).

The legacy shapes are kept as deprecated types: `GitLabConfig` (`config.go:210`) / `GitLabPullConfig` (221), all fields `,omitempty`.

**`docker:` → `network:` is already complete and retired**: there is no `DockerConfig` type and no `yaml:"docker"` tag left in the tree (grep returns nothing); only the comments at `config.go:410` and `forge.go:27` (`docker.network_tool_image`) record it. (`internal/ui/forge/explorer/pipeline.go:92-212`) — canal bufferisé plus un

état qui dure. `Kind.Cancellable()` (`jobs.go:63`) ne liste que scan et pull, et
`Kinds()` est parcouru par un test qui échoue pour un `Kind` sans icône ni
verbe — le coût serait réel pour un mauvais ajustement sémantique.

# §3.1 — Redirecteur de ports non privilégié (4e onglet de `:net`) > À recopier dans `.claude/plans/port-forward-plan.md` au début de > l'implémentation (règle de `.claude/rules/planning.md`). ## Contexte §3.1 du backlog tient en une ligne depuis `todo.md` : « *Port-forwarding manager — an interactive dashboard to manage port redirections to the host machine* ». L'analyse qui précède ce plan a tranché deux choses : 1. **Les alias de noms via `/etc/hosts` sont abandonnés.** Ils demandent une élévation sur les trois plateformes (UAC sous Windows même pour un compte administrateur), trois mécanismes distincts, et une réinvocation auto-élevée qui est une surface d'élévation de privilèges à sécuriser. Cela irait aussi à l'encontre de §3.43/§3.44, qui ont retiré le dernier conteneur privilégié de l'application. 2. **Le redirecteur, lui, ne demande aucun droit.** C'est un `net.Listen` + deux `io.Copy` dans le process DevDesk. Mesuré dans le sandbox Linux : bind refusé sur 80 et 443 en non-root, accepté sur 8080. Windows n'a pas de plage réservée. Se limiter aux ports ≥ 1024 rend la fonctionnalité portable sans privilège. Résultat visé : depuis `:net`, ouvrir un port local vers un `host:port` quelconque — avec pré-remplissage depuis un conteneur en cours d'exécution et ses ports **non publiés**, qui est le cas d'usage qui a le plus de valeur (joindre un service sans redémarrer le conteneur). ## Décisions déjà prises | Question | Réponse | |---|---| | Cible | Proxy TCP générique + pré-remplissage depuis un conteneur | | Persistance | **Session seulement** — rien dans le YAML, aucune migration | | Emplacement | **4e onglet de `:net`**, à côté de Diagnostics / Ports / Interfaces | La persistance session-seulement n'est pas qu'une simplification : un listener ne peut pas survivre au process qui le détient, donc une liste persistée promettrait ce qu'elle ne peut pas tenir. ## Le risque principal — à mesurer AVANT d'écrire le pré-remplissage conteneur **C'est une rechute possible de D55.** `docs/architecture/network.md:181-191` raconte que l'onglet Ports listait les sockets de la VM Docker Desktop en croyant parler de l'hôte, et que `K` tuait un process de la VM. Le mécanisme est le même ici : sous Docker Desktop (Windows, macOS), **l'IP d'un conteneur n'est pas routable depuis l'hôte** — elle l'est sous Docker natif Linux. Un redirecteur qui composerait `172.17.0.2:80` marcherait sur la machine du développeur Linux et échouerait sur celle de l'utilisateur. Deux mesures à faire sur l'**hôte Windows**, avant l'étape 3 : 1. Lancer un conteneur avec un port exposé non publié, lire son IP (`docker inspect`), et tenter un `Test-NetConnection -Port

` depuis l'hôte. C'est la mesure qui décide. 2. Vérifier que `docker inspect` et `podman inspect` s'accordent sur `.NetworkSettings.Networks.*.IPAddress` — même classe de divergence que les trois gabarits trouvés en §3.67. **Ce que le plan fait de ce risque, quelle qu'en soit l'issue** : le redirecteur **sonde** la cible avant d'ouvrir le listener, et rapporte l'échec en nommant la cause probable. Il ne détecte pas la plateforme et ne devine rien — c'est la philosophie de `netcheck` (mesurer, pas supposer), et c'est ce qui empêche un « ça marche chez moi » silencieux. ## Architecture ### Qui détient les listeners — le routeur, jamais la vue `internal/app/app.go:343` : `reinitializeViews` fait `a.views = make(map[...])` à chaque sauvegarde de config et à chaque changement de contexte. **Un listener détenu par le modèle netdiag fuirait à ce moment-là**, sans que rien ne le signale. Le précédent exact est le serveur MCP (`internal/app/mcp.go`) : `net.Listen` dans un `Cmd` (l'I/O appartient au `Cmd`, Rule 110), le handle revient **sur un message**, et `Update` est le seul à le stocker. `sharedState` est créé une fois dans `newWithSize` (`app.go:205`) et muté sur place — il survit donc aux reconstructions de vues. Le modèle à suivre est celui de `internal/jobs`, qui est le plus proche : le routeur détient le registre (`a.jobs = jobs.New()`, `app.go:216`), les vues ne le reçoivent **pas** ; elles émettent un message de demande et reçoivent un **instantané** en retour (`jobs.StartMsg` → `handleStartJobs` → `jobs.ChangedMsg`, `internal/app/jobs.go:18-58`). Les types de messages vivent dans le paquet du domaine, pas dans `internal/app`, pour que les vues puissent les importer sans importer le routeur. ### Nouveau paquet `internal/forward` Aucune dépendance à `internal/docker` ni à l'UI — il ne connaît que des `host:port`. C'est ce qui le rend testable sans conteneur. ```go // Forward is one live redirection, as the table reads it. type Forward struct { ID string // stable across snapshots; the datatable Key LocalPort int Target string // host:port Label string // where it came from: a container name, or empty Opened time.Time Active int // connections currently proxied Total int64 // connections accepted since it opened LastErr string // last dial failure, empty when healthy } type Registry struct { /* mu sync.Mutex; entries map[string]*entry */ } func New() *Registry func (r *Registry) Open(localPort int, target, label string) (Forward, error) func (r *Registry) Close(id string) error func (r *Registry) CloseAll() func (r *Registry) List() []Forward // sorted snapshot, safe to hand to a view ``` Quatre décisions à écrire dans le code, chacune avec son test : - **`Open` écoute sur `127.0.0.1` uniquement, jamais `0.0.0.0`.** Publier sur toutes les interfaces exposerait au LAN un service que le conteneur avait justement gardé pour lui — c'est exactement ce que §3.64 cherche à repérer, et le faire ici par défaut serait contradictoire. Pas d'option pour l'instant. - **Les ports < 1024 sont refusés avant l'appel système**, avec une raison nommée, plutôt que de laisser remonter un `bind: permission denied` qui ne dit pas que la limite est structurelle et sans contournement non privilégié. - **La cible est sondée avant que le listener n'ouvre.** Un `net.DialTimeout` court : ça échoue tout de suite et clairement, plutôt qu'à la première connexion, une fois que l'utilisateur a déjà pointé son client dessus. C'est aussi ce qui attrape le cas Docker Desktop décrit plus haut. - **Les compteurs sont atomiques, et le registre a un mutex** — contrairement à `internal/jobs`, qui n'en a délibérément pas (`registry.go:18-25` : « *a mutex here would say a Cmd may touch it, and that is exactly the thing that must stay untrue* »). La différence est réelle et doit être écrite, sinon elle se lit comme une incohérence : `jobs` n'est muté que depuis `Update`, alors que les goroutines d'accept de ce registre-ci écrivent vraiment dans les compteurs. `mise run test-race` est la vérification qui compte. # §3.1 — Redirecteur de ports non privilégié (4e onglet de `:net`) > À recopier dans `.claude/plans/port-forward-plan.md` au début de > l'implémentation (règle de `.claude/rules/planning.md`). ## Contexte §3.1 du backlog tient en une ligne depuis `todo.md` : « *Port-forwarding manager — an interactive dashboard to manage port redirections to the host machine* ». L'analyse qui précède ce plan a tranché deux choses : 1. **Les alias de noms via `/etc/hosts` sont abandonnés.** Ils demandent une élévation sur les trois plateformes (UAC sous Windows même pour un compte administrateur), trois mécanismes distincts, et une réinvocation auto-élevée qui est une surface d'élévation de privilèges à sécuriser. Cela irait aussi à l'encontre de §3.43/§3.44, qui ont retiré le dernier conteneur privilégié de l'application. 2. **Le redirecteur, lui, ne demande aucun droit.** C'est un `net.Listen` + deux `io.Copy` dans le process DevDesk. Mesuré dans le sandbox Linux : bind refusé sur 80 et 443 en non-root, accepté sur 8080. Windows n'a pas de plage réservée. Se limiter aux ports ≥ 1024 rend la fonctionnalité portable sans privilège. Résultat visé : depuis `:net`, ouvrir un port local vers un `host:port` quelconque — avec pré-remplissage depuis un conteneur en cours d'exécution et ses ports **non publiés**, qui est le cas d'usage qui a le plus de valeur (joindre un service sans redémarrer le conteneur). ## Décisions déjà prises | Question | Réponse | |---|---| | Cible | Proxy TCP générique + pré-remplissage depuis un conteneur | | Persistance | **Session seulement** — rien dans le YAML, aucune migration | | Emplacement | **4e onglet de `:net`**, à côté de Diagnostics / Ports / Interfaces | La persistance session-seulement n'est pas qu'une simplification : un listener ne peut pas survivre au process qui le détient, donc une liste persistée promettrait ce qu'elle ne peut pas tenir. ## Le risque principal — à mesurer AVANT d'écrire le pré-remplissage conteneur **C'est une rechute possible de D55.** `docs/architecture/network.md:181-191` raconte que l'onglet Ports listait les sockets de la VM Docker Desktop en croyant parler de l'hôte, et que `K` tuait un process de la VM. Le mécanisme est le même ici : sous Docker Desktop (Windows, macOS), **l'IP d'un conteneur n'est pas routable depuis l'hôte** — elle l'est sous Docker natif Linux. Un redirecteur qui composerait `172.17.0.2:80` marcherait sur la machine du développeur Linux et échouerait sur celle de l'utilisateur. Deux mesures à faire sur l'**hôte Windows**, avant l'étape 3 : 1. Lancer un conteneur avec un port exposé non publié, lire son IP (`docker inspect`), et tenter un `Test-NetConnection -Port

` depuis l'hôte. C'est la mesure qui décide. 2.
